title: A Survey on the Fairness of Recommender Systems
abstract: Recommender systems are an essential tool to relieve the information overload challenge and play an important role in people’s daily lives. Since recommendations involve allocations of social resources (e.g., job recommendation), an important issue is whether recommendations are fair. Unfair recommendations are not only unethical but also harm the long-term interests of the recommender system itself. As a result, fairness issues in recommender systems have recently attracted increasing attention. However, due to multiple complex resource allocation processes and various fairness definitions, the research on fairness in recommendation is scattered. To fill this gap, we review over 60 papers published in top conferences/journals, including TOIS, SIGIR, and WWW. First, we summarize fairness definitions in the recommendation and provide several views to classify fairness issues. Then, we review recommendation datasets and measurements in fairness studies and provide an elaborate taxonomy of fairness methods in the recommendation. Finally, we conclude this survey by outlining some promising future directions.

claims.text: Recommender systems perform a resource allocation role in society by allocating information to users and exposure to items.
Consistent fairness is the most common definition of fairness used in recommender systems literature.
Current research on fairness in recommendation focuses primarily on group-level fairness rather than individual-level fairness.

Classification-focused machine learning fairness methods cannot be directly applied to recommender systems due to two-sided platform dynamics, feedback loops, personalization, and multi-metric trade-offs.
Improving item fairness in recommender systems can cause user fairness to degrade or remain unchanged.

limitations.text: Research on fairness in recommendation is scattered due to multiple complex resource allocation processes and diverse fairness definitions.
Most user fairness studies in recommender systems evaluate only recommendation accuracy, neglecting non-accuracy measurements such as diversity, unexpectedness, and serendipity.
Existing recommendation datasets lack evaluations on emerging multimodal scenarios like short videos and lack sensitive demographic attributes like race.
Existing fairness methods in recommender systems generally assume all sensitive attributes are fully available, failing when protected user or item attributes are missing.

future_work.text: Establish a general consensus and priority hierarchy among conflicting fairness definitions across different recommendation scenarios.
Develop standardized experimental benchmarks, dataset preprocessing standards, and hyperparameter tuning strategies for recommendation fairness evaluation.
Investigate fairness issues and collect datasets for emerging multi-modal recommendation scenarios such as short video recommendations.
Design algorithms that improve fairness while maintaining recommendation accuracy to avoid commercial utility loss.
Develop learnable re-ranking algorithms and multi-objective optimization strategies to simultaneously satisfy user fairness and item fairness.
Apply causal inference techniques to model complex feature relationships and eliminate unfairness under missing demographic attribute data.
Develop theoretical and causal methods to explain why unfairness occurs in recommender systems.
